label: Opening Hook
text: For two hundred years, Roman emperors, poets, and travelers sailed up the Nile just to hear a 60-foot stone titan sing to the sunrise.
title: File:Colossi of Memnon R01.jpg

label: Terrain & Scale
text: The two monolithic quartz-sandstone statues depicting Pharaoh Amenhotep III were erected in the 14th century BC to guard his mortuary temple.
title: File:Colossal statues of Memnon, seen during the flooding of the Wellcome V0049353.jpg

label: Inner Structure
text: After an earthquake in 27 BC shattered the northern colossus, the fractured stone began emitting a high-pitched tone at dawn, compared by classical witnesses to a harp string or trumpet.
title: Gournah (Thèbes), Colosses (Celui de Droite, Dit de Memnon) (The Met 261839)

label: Physical Evidence
text: Over 100 ancient travelers carved graffiti into the stone base certifying that they personally heard the titan sing.
title: Colossal Statue of  Amenhotep III, reworked, reinscribed by Merneptah (The Met 544479)

label: Survey / Blueprint
text: Physics explains the sound as escaping air and steam generated by rapid morning thermal expansion of dew trapped inside internal stone fissures.
title: File:Colossi of Memnon R02.jpg

label: Anomaly & Debate
text: The acoustic phenomenon permanently ceased around 199 AD when Emperor Septimius Severus attempted to restore the statue by patching the fractures, inadvertently sealing the acoustic vents.
title: Colosse restauré d' Aménophis III, à Thèbes (Statue vocale ou Colosse de Memnon) (The Met 287139)
